title: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
bigQuestion: What is the Tanakh, and how do Jewish communities read it?

story.title: A Scroll That Takes a Year
story.kicker: Every Saturday, one more piece of a very long scroll is read out loud.
paragraphs: It is Saturday morning in a synagogue on the North Side of Chicago. A synagogue is a Jewish house of prayer and study. At the front of the room is a tall cabinet with a curtain. The curtain slides open. Inside stand several scrolls, each one wrapped in a cloth cover.

A woman lifts one scroll out. It is heavy. She carries it to a table and unrolls it a little. The scroll is not paper. It is parchment, made from animal skin. Every letter on it was written by hand with a quill. There are no pictures and no page numbers.

A boy named Eli watches from the third row. He asks his aunt, "Why don't they just read the whole thing?" His aunt smiles. "It is too long," she whispers. "We read one piece each week. It takes a whole year to reach the end."

The reader touches the parchment with a small silver pointer shaped like a hand. She does not touch the letters with her finger. Then she begins to chant, slowly, in Hebrew. Eli cannot understand the words yet. But he can hear that this is not ordinary reading.

After the reading, the scroll is rolled up, dressed again and carried back to the cabinet. Eli's aunt tells him that next Saturday the reading will start right where it stopped. "And when we finish the last line," she says, "we go straight back to the first one."
story.think: Why do you think Jewish communities read the scroll one piece at a time, instead of all at once?

lessons.title: What the Name Tanakh Means
lessons.mainIdea: Tanakh is a name built from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim.
reading: The Hebrew Bible has a short name: *Tanakh*. The name is a bit like a code. It is made from three first letters: T, N and K. Each letter stands for one part of the book. Put the three parts together and you have the whole Tanakh.

The T is for *Torah*. Torah means "teaching." The N is for *Nevi'im*. That word means "prophets." A prophet is a person who brings a message from God, as the tradition tells it. The K is for *Ketuvim*. That word means "writings." It holds songs, sayings and stories.

Jewish tradition puts the three parts in this order: Torah first, then Nevi'im, then Ketuvim. The Torah comes first because Jewish tradition treats it as the heart of the whole book. In this course we will read all three parts, in that order.

words.d: the Hebrew Bible; a name made from the first letters of Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
"teaching"; the first part of the Tanakh, five books long
"prophets"; the second part of the Tanakh
"writings"; the third part of the Tanakh

look.title: Build the Name
look.text: Torah starts with T. Nevi'im starts with N. Ketuvim starts with K. In Hebrew the three letters are tav, nun and kaf. Say the three letters together with some vowels in between, and you get Ta-Na-Kh. Now imagine a school with three parts: Art, Math and Science. What short name could you build from those first letters?
look.prompt: Make up a three-part name for something you know, using its first letters, and explain what each letter stands for.

check.q: What does the word Tanakh come from?
choices: The first letters of Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
The name of the person who wrote it
The city where it was first printed
check.why: Tanakh is built from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim.

check.q: What does the word Nevi'im mean?
check.why: Nevi'im means "prophets." It is the second part of the Tanakh.

check.q: Which part of the Tanakh comes first in Jewish tradition?
check.why: The Torah is first. Jewish tradition treats it as the heart of the whole book.

lessons.title: Twenty-Four Books
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition counts 24 books in the Tanakh: five in the Torah, eight in Nevi'im and eleven in Ketuvim.
reading: Jewish tradition counts twenty-four books in the Tanakh. The Torah has five books. Nevi'im has eight. Ketuvim has eleven. Five plus eight plus eleven makes twenty-four. Some of these books are long. Some are only a page or two.

The five books of the Torah are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Those are the English names. Each book also has a Hebrew name. You will learn the Hebrew names in the next chapter. Together the five books tell one long story.

Nevi'im holds books named for prophets, like Isaiah and Jeremiah. It also holds history books, like Joshua and Kings. Ketuvim holds Psalms, which are songs, and Proverbs, which are wise sayings. It also holds short books like Ruth and Esther. The very last book is Chronicles.

words.d: one of the 24 parts of the Tanakh, such as Genesis or Psalms
the first book of the Torah; its Hebrew name is Bereshit
the last book of the Tanakh, found at the end of Ketuvim

look.title: How Many Books in Each Part
look.cite: Traditional Jewish count of the books of the Tanakh, as in the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b
look.prompt: Add the first three rows. Do they match the last row? Which part has the most books?

check.q: How many books does Jewish tradition count in the Tanakh?
check.why: The traditional Jewish count is 24 books: 5 in the Torah, 8 in Nevi'im and 11 in Ketuvim.

check.q: Which book is the very last one in the Tanakh?
check.why: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles, the last book of Ketuvim.

check.q: Which of these books is in the Torah?
check.why: Leviticus is one of the five books of the Torah. Psalms and Ruth are in Ketuvim, and Isaiah is in Nevi'im.

lessons.title: What Each Part Holds
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah tells the story from creation to Moses, Nevi'im tells of the land and the prophets, and Ketuvim holds songs, sayings and scrolls.
reading: The three parts of the Tanakh hold different kinds of writing. The *Torah* is mostly story and law. It begins with the creation of the world. It ends with the death of Moses, just before the people enter the land. Jewish tradition calls the whole thing "the teaching."

*Nevi'im*, the prophets, comes in two halves. The first half is history. It tells how the people entered the land, chose kings and, later, lost the land. The second half holds the words of prophets. A *prophet* speaks a message that, as the tradition tells it, comes from God. The message is often hard to hear.

*Ketuvim*, the writings, is the most mixed part. It has songs, called Psalms. It has wise sayings, called Proverbs. It has a poem about love and a poem about grief. It has stories about a queen and about a man in a lions' den. It ends with a history that looks back over everything.

words.d: a person who, as Jewish tradition tells it, brings a message from God to the people
a book of 150 songs and poems in Ketuvim

look.title: Sort the Books
look.text: Here are six books: Genesis, Isaiah, Psalms, Joshua, Esther, Deuteronomy. Two are in the Torah, which tells the story from creation to Moses. Two are in Nevi'im, which holds history and prophets. Two are in Ketuvim, which holds songs, sayings and short stories. Use the hints: Genesis is the first book of all. Deuteronomy holds Moses's last words. Joshua takes over from Moses. Isaiah is a prophet. Psalms are songs. Esther is a queen.
look.prompt: Put each of the six books in its part, and say one clue that helped you.

check.q: Which part of the Tanakh holds the Psalms?
choices: None of them; Psalms is a separate book
check.why: Psalms is in Ketuvim, the writings, along with Proverbs, Ruth and Esther.

check.q: How does the Torah end?
choices: With the building of the Temple
With the story of Queen Esther
With the creation of the world
check.why: The Torah ends with the death of Moses, just before the people enter the land. The Temple and Esther come later.

check.q: What is a prophet, as Jewish tradition tells it?
choices: A person who brings a message from God
A king who rules the land
check.why: In Jewish tradition a prophet is a messenger. The books of Nevi'im carry those messages.

lessons.title: The Language of the Tanakh
lessons.mainIdea: The Tanakh was written mostly in Hebrew, with a few parts in a related language called Aramaic.
reading: Almost all of the Tanakh was written in *Hebrew*. Hebrew is an old language. It is still spoken today in Israel. Many Jewish children in Chicago learn some Hebrew so they can read the Tanakh and the prayers. Hebrew has its own alphabet with twenty-two letters.

A few parts of the Tanakh are in *Aramaic*. Aramaic is a cousin of Hebrew. Long ago, many people in the Middle East spoke it. Some chapters in the book of Daniel are in Aramaic. So are some parts of the book of Ezra. Scholars can tell the two languages apart.

Because the Tanakh is in Hebrew, people who read English use a *translation*. A translation says the same thing in a new language. This course uses a translation made in 1917. Translators try hard to be faithful. But every translation makes some choices, and no translation is the Hebrew itself.

words.d: the language of almost all of the Tanakh; still spoken in Israel today
a language related to Hebrew, used in a few parts of Daniel and Ezra
the same words said again in a different language

look.title: Letters in Three Alphabets
look.cite: Standard letter counts of the Hebrew, English and Greek alphabets
look.prompt: Which alphabet has the fewest letters? How many more letters does English have than Hebrew?

check.q: In what language was almost all of the Tanakh written?
check.why: The Tanakh is almost all in Hebrew, with a few parts in Aramaic.

check.q: Which books have some chapters in Aramaic?
check.why: Parts of Daniel and parts of Ezra are in Aramaic, a language related to Hebrew.

check.q: How many letters are in the Hebrew alphabet?
check.why: The Hebrew alphabet has 22 letters. English has 26.

lessons.title: Reading From Right to Left
lessons.mainIdea: Hebrew is read from right to left, and a Torah scroll is written without vowel marks.
reading: English goes from left to right across the page. Hebrew goes the other way. You start at the right edge and read toward the left. A Hebrew book opens from what looks like the back to an English reader. When a Torah scroll is unrolled, the reading moves from the right roller to the left one.

Here is something surprising. A Torah scroll is written with almost no *vowels*. Vowels are the sounds like a, e, i, o and u. In Hebrew, most vowels are small dots and dashes placed under or above the letters. A scroll leaves them out. The reader has to know the words already.

Children's Hebrew books do have the vowel dots. So do most printed Hebrew Bibles. Those dots were added by careful scholars long after the Tanakh was written. Reading from a scroll without them takes a lot of practice. That is why the reader in a synagogue studies the passage all week before Saturday.

words.d: a sound like a, e, i, o or u; in Hebrew, mostly shown by small dots and dashes
the direction Hebrew is read, the opposite of English

look.title: Words Without Vowels
look.text: Try reading this English sentence with the vowels taken out: TH TRH S RD N SHBBT. Can you figure it out? It says: THE TORAH IS READ ON SHABBAT. It is easier if you already know what the sentence is about. Readers of a Torah scroll face this on every line, and in Hebrew. That is why they practice the reading all week.
look.prompt: Write your own name and one short sentence without vowels. Trade with a partner. Was it easy or hard to read?

check.q: In which direction is Hebrew read?
check.why: Hebrew is read from right to left, the opposite of English.

check.q: What does a Torah scroll leave out?
check.why: A Torah scroll is written with the letters only. The vowel dots and dashes are left out, so the reader must know the words.

check.q: Why does a synagogue reader practice the passage all week?
choices: Because the scroll is in English
Because the scroll has pictures to explain
Because the scroll has no vowel marks and must be read correctly
Because the reading changes every day
check.why: Without vowel marks, the reader must already know the words. Practice makes the reading correct.

lessons.title: A Scribe and a Quill
lessons.mainIdea: A Torah scroll is written by hand on parchment by a trained scribe, and it must have no mistakes.
reading: A Torah scroll is not printed by a machine. It is written by hand. The person who writes it is called a *scribe*. In Hebrew, a scribe is a *sofer*. A sofer trains for years. The work is slow and careful. One scroll can take a year or more to finish.

The scroll is made of *parchment*. Parchment is animal skin that has been cleaned and stretched until it is smooth. The sofer writes with a quill, which is a feather cut to a point, and with special black ink. Sheets of parchment are sewn together and attached to two wooden rollers.

Jewish tradition says every letter must be correct. If a sofer makes a mistake, it must be fixed before the scroll can be used. A scroll with a broken letter is set aside until it is repaired. This care is one reason the words of the Tanakh have stayed so steady across hundreds of years.

words.d: a person trained to write a Torah scroll by hand; in Hebrew, a sofer
animal skin made smooth for writing on
a feather cut to a point and dipped in ink for writing

look.title: Reading the Torah Aloud to Everyone
look.text: The book of Nehemiah tells of a day when the people gathered in Jerusalem. Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform and read from the scroll of the Torah from early morning until midday. The people stood and listened. Helpers explained the reading so that everyone understood it.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:1–8, Jewish Publication Society translation (1917), retold in plain words
look.prompt: Ezra was called a scribe. What two jobs does this passage show a scribe doing?

check.q: What is a sofer?
choices: A scribe who writes Torah scrolls
check.why: Sofer is the Hebrew word for a scribe, the trained person who writes a Torah scroll by hand.

check.q: What is a Torah scroll written on?
check.why: A Torah scroll is written on parchment, animal skin that has been cleaned and stretched smooth.

check.q: What happens if a scribe makes a mistake in a scroll?
choices: It must be fixed before the scroll can be used
The scribe starts a new job
check.why: Jewish tradition says every letter must be correct, so a mistake must be repaired before the scroll is read.

lessons.title: The Pointer and the Ark
lessons.mainIdea: In a synagogue the Torah scroll rests in a cabinet called the ark, and the reader follows the words with a pointer called a yad.
reading: In a synagogue, the Torah scrolls live in a special cabinet at the front of the room. It is called the *ark*. In Hebrew it is the *aron kodesh*, the holy cabinet. A curtain or a door covers it. When the ark is opened, people in many synagogues stand up.

Each scroll is dressed. It wears a cloth cover, and sometimes a silver crown or a breastplate. When it is time to read, the scroll is carried to a table and undressed. Then it is unrolled to the right place. The reader does not touch the letters with a finger. Fingers can smudge the ink.

Instead, the reader uses a *yad*. Yad means "hand" in Hebrew. A yad is a thin pointer, often made of silver, with a tiny hand at the tip. The reader moves the yad along the line while chanting. After the reading, the scroll is rolled up, dressed again and carried back to the ark.

words.d: the cabinet at the front of a synagogue where the Torah scrolls are kept; in Hebrew, aron kodesh
"hand"; a pointer used to follow the words on a Torah scroll
a Jewish house of prayer and study

look.text: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.
look.prompt: This line is written inside the Torah scroll and is also said in Jewish prayer. Why might a community keep a sentence in a scroll and also say it every day?

choices: The cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept
check.why: The ark, or aron kodesh, is the cabinet at the front of the synagogue that holds the Torah scrolls. Noah's ark is a different word in Hebrew.

check.q: Why does the reader use a yad instead of a finger?
choices: Because the scroll is too far away
Because Hebrew is read right to left
Because the yad reads the words out loud
Because fingers can smudge the ink
check.why: The yad is a pointer that keeps the reader's fingers off the letters, so the ink is not smudged.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word yad mean?
check.why: Yad means "hand." The pointer often has a tiny hand at its tip.

lessons.title: The Weekly Portion
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah is divided into weekly portions, called parashot, so the whole scroll is read aloud over one year.
reading: The Torah is long. To read it all, Jewish communities split it into pieces. Each piece is called a *parashah*. That word means "portion" or "section." One parashah is read aloud each week, on Shabbat morning. The plural is parashot.

Most years there are fifty-four portions on the list. Some years have fewer weeks, so two short portions are read together. Each parashah has a name. The name comes from one of its first words. The first parashah is called Bereshit, "In the beginning," because Genesis starts with that word.

Each week many Jewish families and schools talk about that week's parashah. A child might hear the story of Noah one week and the story of Abraham a few weeks later. Because the cycle is the same each year, the stories come around again and again. Children grow up with them.

words.d: "portion"; the section of the Torah read aloud in one week
the seventh day of the week, a day of rest; the Torah portion is read on Shabbat morning
a set of things that repeats in the same order, like the weekly Torah readings

look.title: The Yearly Reading
look.cite: The standard yearly cycle of Torah portions used in synagogues today; in some years two portions are read on one Shabbat
look.prompt: There are 54 portions but only 52 weeks. What must happen in some weeks?

check.q: What is a parashah?
choices: The section of the Torah read in one week
The cabinet that holds the scroll
check.why: A parashah is a weekly portion. One is read aloud each Shabbat.

check.q: How does a parashah get its name?
choices: From the scribe who wrote it
From the number of its chapter
From one of its first words
From the holiday nearest to it
check.why: Each portion is named for one of its first words. Bereshit is named for the first word of Genesis.

check.q: About how long does it take to read the whole Torah in the yearly cycle?
check.why: One portion is read each week, so the whole Torah is finished in about one year.

lessons.title: Simchat Torah: Ending and Starting
lessons.mainIdea: On the holiday of Simchat Torah, Jewish communities finish the last words of the Torah and immediately begin again at the first.
reading: The yearly cycle ends and begins on one holiday. It is called *Simchat Torah*. The name means "rejoicing in the Torah." It comes in the fall, right after the holiday of Sukkot. On that day the last portion of Deuteronomy is read aloud. Then, without a pause, the first portion of Genesis is read.

Simchat Torah is a joyful day. In many synagogues, people take all the scrolls out of the ark. They carry them around the room while singing. They dance with them. Children often walk in the parade holding flags. Everyone celebrates that a whole year of reading is done.

Why start again right away? Jewish tradition teaches that the study of Torah never ends. The last word of Deuteronomy leads back to the first word of Genesis. A person who has read the Torah many times can still find something new. So the scroll is rolled all the way back, and the reading begins again.

words.d: "rejoicing in the Torah"; the fall holiday when the yearly reading ends and begins again
a fall harvest holiday; Simchat Torah comes right after it
the fifth and last book of the Torah; its Hebrew name is Devarim

look.title: Last Line, First Line
look.text: Picture a synagogue on Simchat Torah. A reader chants the last words of Deuteronomy, about the death of Moses. People call out with joy. A second scroll is already open on the table, rolled to the very beginning. The reader chants: In the beginning. The scroll is heavy, but people take turns carrying the scrolls around the room while others clap and sing.
look.prompt: Why might a community celebrate the end of a book by starting it again instead of putting it away?

check.q: What happens on Simchat Torah?
choices: The last portion of the Torah is read and the first portion begins again
The scrolls are put away for the winter
The Psalms are sung all day
check.why: On Simchat Torah the reading of Deuteronomy ends and the reading of Genesis begins right away.

check.q: What does Simchat Torah mean?
check.why: Simchat Torah means "rejoicing in the Torah." It is a joyful holiday with singing and dancing.

check.q: When does Simchat Torah come?

lessons.title: Same Books, Different Order
lessons.mainIdea: Christians call these books the Old Testament and arrange them in a different order; this course follows the Tanakh's order and the JPS translation of 1917.
reading: The books of the Tanakh are also holy books for Christians. Christians call them the *Old Testament*. The words inside are the same books. But the order is different, and the count is different. Christians usually list thirty-nine books, because they split some books that Jewish tradition counts as one. Samuel, for example, becomes First Samuel and Second Samuel.

The order matters. The Tanakh ends with Chronicles, which looks back and ends with a call to return home to Jerusalem. The Christian Old Testament ends with the prophet Malachi. Each tradition arranges the books in the way that fits how it reads them. This course keeps the Tanakh's order: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim.

This course reads an English translation called the *JPS 1917*. JPS stands for the Jewish Publication Society. In 1917 a group of Jewish scholars in Philadelphia finished it. It was the first time a group of American Jewish scholars worked together to translate the whole Tanakh into English. Its English sounds old, with words like "thou" and "unto," but it is careful and free for anyone to use.

words.d: the Christian name for the books of the Tanakh, arranged in a different order
the English translation of the Tanakh made by the Jewish Publication Society in 1917; the one this course reads
